questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=12{x}^{2}-6$ and $f(1)=-2.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=1$ to estimate the value of $f(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(1)=-2,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=12{x}^{2}-6,$ then ${f}^{′}(1)=12(1)^{2}-6=6.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=-2+6(x-1).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(2)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & ≈L(2) \\  & =-2+6(2-1) \\  & =-2+6(1) \\  & =-2+6 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that the tangent line approximation to the function $f(x)$ at $x=3$ underestimates the function in the neighborhood of $x=3,$ which of the following must be true?
questions.worked_solution:
Since the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=3$ underestimates the values of this function in the neighborhood of $x=3$, we have

$$
L(x)<f(x),
$$

for all $x$ close to (but not equal to) $x=3.$ In other words, the line $L(x)$ must be *below* the graph of $f(x)$ near the point  $x=3.$

Therefore, the function must be concave up in the neighborhood of $x=3.$

questions.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(0,5)$ and is concave down on the interval $(-\pi ,\pi ).$ If ${f}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},$ estimate the value of $f(\sqrt{2})$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=0$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(0,5),$ so we have $f(0)=5.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =5+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x-0) \\  & =5+\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(\sqrt{2})$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=\sqrt{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{2}) & ≈L(\sqrt{2}) \\  & =5+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =5+1 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(-\pi ,\pi ),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=0,$ and therefore we have an overestimate.

The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(2)=5,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=3{x}^{2}-2x,$ we have

$$
{f}^{′}(2)=3(2)^{2}-2(2)=12-4=8.
$$

So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=5+8(x-2).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(2.4)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=2.4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2.4) & ≈L(2.4) \\  & =5+8(2.4-2) \\  & =5+8(0.4) \\  & =5+3.2 \\  & =8.2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(0,1)$ and is concave up on the interval $(-1,2).$ If ${f}^{′}(0)=1,$ estimate the value of $f(-0.3)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=0$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.

$\,f(-0.3)≈$ {{field-1}} and the approximation is an {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0).\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of the function passes through the point $(0,1),$ so we have $f(0)=1.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(0)=1.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =1+1(x-0) \\  & =1+x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(-0.3)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=-0.3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-0.3) & ≈L(-0.3) \\  & =1+(-0.3) \\  & =0.7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave up on the interval $(-1,2),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is below the graph near $x=0,$ and therefore we have an $\text{underestimate}.$
